articles.title: Major BGP routing incident affects multiple regions
articles.author: elira-hoxha
articles.summary: A route leak from a regional transit provider caused traffic for several content networks to take unusual paths for about 40 minutes.
articles.imageAlt: Editorial illustration for networking story: BGP

brief.what: A route leak from a regional transit provider caused traffic for several content networks to take unusual paths for about 40 minutes.
brief.who: Users in several regions reported slow or failed connections to affected services during the incident.
brief.why: Users may see slow or failed connections to services whose prefixes were affected, even though the services themselves remain healthy.
brief.next: The transit provider says it has corrected the filter configuration that allowed the leak.

articles.whyItMatters: Users may see slow or failed connections to services whose prefixes were affected, even though the services themselves remain healthy. Network operators should validate RPKI filtering, review max-prefix limits and confirm that monitoring alerts on unexpected origin changes.

sections.heading: Summary
paragraphs: A route leak from a regional transit provider caused traffic for several content networks to take unusual paths for about 40 minutes.
Monitoring data shows more-specific prefixes propagating through networks that did not enforce strict customer filtering.

sections.heading: Technical Analysis
paragraphs: The Border Gateway Protocol relies largely on trust between networks; an incorrect announcement can propagate widely within minutes.
Route leaks and mis-originations are usually mitigated by RPKI route-origin validation and strict prefix filtering at network edges.

sections.heading: Impact
paragraphs: Users may see slow or failed connections to services whose prefixes were affected, even though the services themselves remain healthy.
Users in several regions reported slow or failed connections to affected services during the incident.

sections.heading: What you should know
paragraphs: Network operators should validate RPKI filtering, review max-prefix limits and confirm that monitoring alerts on unexpected origin changes.
The transit provider says it has corrected the filter configuration that allowed the leak.

articles.author: elira-hoxha
articles.summary: Enterprise access point vendors are shipping firmware that enables multi-link operation for supported clients.

brief.what: Enterprise access point vendors are shipping firmware that enables multi-link operation for supported clients.
brief.who: Benefits apply only to clients that support the feature, which remain a minority in most fleets.
brief.why: Benefits depend on client support; mixed fleets will see gains only on devices that implement the new capabilities.
brief.next: Vendors expect broader client support as laptop refresh cycles continue.

articles.whyItMatters: Benefits depend on client support; mixed fleets will see gains only on devices that implement the new capabilities. Plan upgrades around client refresh cycles, validate wired uplink capacity and re-run site surveys before large rollouts.

sections.heading: Summary
paragraphs: Enterprise access point vendors are shipping firmware that enables multi-link operation for supported clients.
Multi-link operation allows a client to transmit over more than one band simultaneously.

sections.heading: Technical Analysis
paragraphs: Enterprise wireless design balances client capacity, roaming performance and channel planning across dense office environments.
Multi-link operation lets a client use more than one band at once, which can reduce latency and improve resilience against interference.

sections.heading: Impact
paragraphs: Benefits depend on client support; mixed fleets will see gains only on devices that implement the new capabilities.
Benefits apply only to clients that support the feature, which remain a minority in most fleets.

sections.heading: What you should know
paragraphs: Plan upgrades around client refresh cycles, validate wired uplink capacity and re-run site surveys before large rollouts.

articles.title: ISP outage disrupts connectivity across multiple regions
articles.author: elira-hoxha
articles.summary: A regional internet provider restored service after a core routing fault disconnected business and residential customers.
articles.imageAlt: Editorial illustration for networking story: Network Outages

brief.what: A regional internet provider restored service after a core routing fault disconnected business and residential customers.
brief.who: Business customers without backup connections lost connectivity for about two hours.
brief.why: Businesses without a secondary connection experience complete loss of connectivity for the duration of the incident.
brief.next: The provider says it will publish a post-incident report.

articles.whyItMatters: Businesses without a secondary connection experience complete loss of connectivity for the duration of the incident. Consider diverse secondary links, SD-WAN failover and documented escalation contacts with providers.

sections.heading: Summary
paragraphs: A regional internet provider restored service after a core routing fault disconnected business and residential customers.
The provider says a configuration change during maintenance triggered the outage.

sections.heading: Technical Analysis
paragraphs: Regional ISP outages often stem from a single failure in core routing, power or fibre infrastructure.
Recovery time depends on redundancy in the provider's backbone and on whether the fault is logical (configuration) or physical (fibre cut).

sections.heading: Impact
paragraphs: Businesses without a secondary connection experience complete loss of connectivity for the duration of the incident.
Business customers without backup connections lost connectivity for about two hours.

sections.heading: What you should know
paragraphs: Consider diverse secondary links, SD-WAN failover and documented escalation contacts with providers.
The provider says it will publish a post-incident report.

articles.title: SD-WAN buyers weigh SASE convergence against vendor lock-in
articles.author: elira-hoxha
articles.summary: Organisations renewing SD-WAN contracts are evaluating whether to move to single-vendor SASE platforms.
articles.imageAlt: Editorial illustration for networking story: SD-WAN

brief.what: Organisations renewing SD-WAN contracts are evaluating whether to move to single-vendor SASE platforms.
brief.who: Enterprises with large branch estates face the most complex decisions.
brief.why: Organisations with long MPLS contracts or complex on-premises security stacks face the largest migration effort.
brief.next: Expect more dual-vendor designs where security and connectivity are procured separately.

articles.whyItMatters: Organisations with long MPLS contracts or complex on-premises security stacks face the largest migration effort. Map application flows first, evaluate exit costs and insist on standards-based interoperability where possible.

sections.heading: Summary
paragraphs: Organisations renewing SD-WAN contracts are evaluating whether to move to single-vendor SASE platforms.
Single-vendor platforms simplify operations but make future vendor changes more costly.

sections.heading: Technical Analysis
paragraphs: SD-WAN replaced many MPLS networks by steering traffic across multiple internet and private links based on application policy.
Secure access service edge (SASE) combines SD-WAN with cloud-delivered security, which changes procurement from boxes to subscriptions.

sections.heading: Impact
paragraphs: Organisations with long MPLS contracts or complex on-premises security stacks face the largest migration effort.
Enterprises with large branch estates face the most complex decisions.

sections.heading: What you should know
paragraphs: Map application flows first, evaluate exit costs and insist on standards-based interoperability where possible.
Expect more dual-vendor designs where security and connectivity are procured separately.

articles.title: Operators report OSPF adjacency flaps after firmware upgrades
articles.author: elira-hoxha
articles.summary: Several network operators describe OSPF adjacencies flapping after routine firmware upgrades on core switches.
articles.imageAlt: Editorial illustration for networking story: OSPF

brief.what: Several network operators describe OSPF adjacencies flapping after routine firmware upgrades on core switches.
brief.who: Networks with mixed firmware versions across OSPF neighbours are most affected.
brief.why: Flapping adjacencies trigger repeated SPF calculations and can cause brief traffic loss across the area.
brief.next: A vendor field notice recommends explicitly configuring MTU on affected interfaces.

articles.whyItMatters: Flapping adjacencies trigger repeated SPF calculations and can cause brief traffic loss across the area. Pin critical parameters explicitly in configuration, compare running defaults before and after upgrades, and alert on adjacency changes.

sections.heading: Summary
paragraphs: Several network operators describe OSPF adjacencies flapping after routine firmware upgrades on core switches.
Initial analysis points to changed MTU handling defaults between releases.

sections.heading: Technical Analysis
paragraphs: OSPF adjacencies depend on matching timers, MTU, area settings and authentication on both neighbours.
Firmware upgrades can change defaults such as MTU handling or authentication behaviour, which causes adjacencies to flap.

sections.heading: Impact
paragraphs: Flapping adjacencies trigger repeated SPF calculations and can cause brief traffic loss across the area.
Networks with mixed firmware versions across OSPF neighbours are most affected.

sections.heading: What you should know
paragraphs: Pin critical parameters explicitly in configuration, compare running defaults before and after upgrades, and alert on adjacency changes.
A vendor field notice recommends explicitly configuring MTU on affected interfaces.

articles.author: elira-hoxha

articles.imageAlt: Editorial illustration for networking story: Internet Infrastructure

brief.what: A repair ship has restored a damaged undersea cable segment, returning capacity to a regional route.
brief.who: Users in the region should see latency return to previous levels.
brief.why: Users in regions with few cable landings are most affected by single cable faults.
brief.next: The cable operator says the cause of the damage is under investigation.

articles.whyItMatters: Users in regions with few cable landings are most affected by single cable faults. Carriers and large enterprises should understand the physical diversity of their international paths.

sections.heading: Summary
paragraphs: A repair ship has restored a damaged undersea cable segment, returning capacity to a regional route.
Traffic had been rerouted over longer paths during the repair, increasing latency for some users.

sections.heading: Technical Analysis
paragraphs: Most intercontinental traffic travels over undersea cables, and repairs require specialised ships and suitable weather.
When a cable fails, traffic shifts to alternative routes, which can increase latency until capacity is restored.

sections.heading: Impact
paragraphs: Users in regions with few cable landings are most affected by single cable faults.
Users in the region should see latency return to previous levels.

sections.heading: What you should know
paragraphs: Carriers and large enterprises should understand the physical diversity of their international paths.
